title: The thirty-three swayyas
hookLine: verses on true devotion and against empty ritual

cards: A uniform tells you what someone is supposed to be. It doesn't tell you what they are. A white coat, a badge, a robe, a turban, a cross on a chain: each one makes a promise on the outside.
Traditions have had to ask what happens when the outside and the inside don't match. Guru Gobind Singh asks it in a set of verses in a form called the swayya.
There are thirty-three of them, and they keep circling one question: what does real devotion look like, under the clothes?

teach.b: A swayya is a verse form, a stanza with a strong, rolling beat, good for reciting aloud. The thirty-three swayyas sit among Guru Gobind Singh's writings, and the first one says who is Khalsa.

teach.h: THE LIGHT THAT NEVER GOES OUT.
teach.b: Paraphrased: the one who remembers, day and night, the light that never goes out; who brings no one but the One into the mind; who is full of love and trust; who does not, even by mistake, put faith in fasts, tombs, shrines and outward rites; who knows the One beyond pilgrimage, charity, austerity and self-control.
When that perfect light shines in the heart, know that one as Khalsa, pure. The light comes first. The love and trust come next.
The outward things are not mocked for fun; they're simply moved out of the center.
Pilgrimage and charity aren't called evil. They're called not enough, on their own, without the One. Other swayyas in the set are sharper.
They turn on people who wear religious dress to impress, or to collect money from the faithful, while their hearts are elsewhere. That edge isn't aimed at one community.

teach.h: A MIRROR FOR YOUR OWN HOUSE.
teach.b: It's aimed at a habit any community can fall into, Sikhs included, and some Sikh teachers read it that way: as a mirror for their own house first.
The verses ask a hard, simple thing. Not, what do you wear, or where have you traveled, but is the light awake inside?

how: Sikhs recite the first of Guru Gobind Singh's thirty-three swayyas when teaching what it means to be Khalsa, and the set is read in katha as a call to inner devotion over outward show.

o: verses listing the rules for a Sikh's dress
verses sung to welcome a new Guru to the court
verses asking what real devotion looks like inside

games.q: the swayyas and their teaching: tap the pairs.
p: a verse with a strong, rolling beat

s: the first swayya calls pilgrimage and charity evil
it moves them out of the center: not enough on their own, without the One.
in the first swayya, the Khalsa is the one in whom the perfect light shines
when that light shines in the heart, know that one as Khalsa.
the sharper swayyas are aimed at one particular community
they target a habit any community can fall into, Sikhs included.

games.q: you're describing the Khalsa in a single verse. what do you put first?
o: the right clothes and the right rites.
remembering the light that never goes out.
the places a person has traveled to on pilgrimage.
games.why: the first swayya begins with remembering the ever-awake light, day and night. the outward things come later, and are called not enough on their own.

practice: Read the first of the thirty-three slowly, once, in any language, or take the paraphrase you just heard.

Then ask, gently, which of your habits are outside and which are inside, without judging either list, and rest your attention on the breath as if it were a small light that doesn't go out. If you pray, say Waheguru on the breath.

wordCard.voice: The thirty-three swayyas. Verses by Guru Gobind Singh on true devotion; the first says the Khalsa is the one in whom the perfect light shines. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Khalsa. the first swayya says who deserves the name: the one in whom the perfect light shines.

carryVoice: Your line: true devotion. Outward things aren't evil, just not enough on their own. Until tomorrow.
